turns.prompt_text: I'm using Fish on Terminal on Mac. It would be nice if I could have a background video going on my terminal. In the past, I've used iTerm2 to have a jellyfish video shown in the background because I like the fish tank aquatic vibe. Is there something similar I could do? I really like getting a high-definition video running in the background. I download the video and play it on a loop, or I'll just play YouTube in the background. However, I prefer not to use the data and just download a video at a high resolution, run it as a loop.
turns.response_html:
Moving toward a high-definition, looped video background is a great way to lean into that "aquatic tank" aesthetic, especially since you’re already using the Fish shell.

Since the shell itself (Fish) only handles the text and logic, the background video is actually a feature of the Terminal Emulator (the window application). If you are looking for an alternative to iTerm2 that handles high-res video loops gracefully on macOS, there are two primary paths: sticking with a GUI-based terminal or using a GPU-accelerated one.

1. The iTerm2 Native Method (Recommended)

Since you’ve used iTerm2 before, it remains the gold standard for this on Mac because it allows per-profile background videos with adjustable transparency.

  • Setup: Go to Settings > Profiles > Window.
  • Background Image: Click the checkbox for Background Image. Instead of a photo, select your downloaded .mp4 or .mov jellyfish video.
  • Optimization: Set the Blending slider. This allows you to dim the video so your terminal text remains readable without losing that high-definition "pop."
  • Looping: iTerm2 automatically loops video files chosen here.

2. Cool Retro Term (The "Vibe" Choice)

If you want something that feels more like an immersive installation, Cool Retro Term is a hardware-accelerated terminal that mimics old cathode-ray tube monitors but allows for heavy customization.

  • It excels at "shimmer" and "bloom" effects that look incredible with aquatic videos.
  • It is less "professional" for daily coding but unmatched for the aesthetic you're describing.

3. The "Video Overlay" Hack (Universal)

If you decide to switch to a terminal that doesn't support video backgrounds natively (like Alacritty or Kitty), you can use a macOS transparency trick:

  1. Download a Video Player with "Float on Top": Use VLC or IINA.
  2. Set Terminal Transparency: In your terminal settings, set the background opacity to 50–70%.
  3. Layering: Place your video player behind the terminal window.
  4. Looping: In IINA or VLC, press the loop button. This gives you high-definition playback without taxing the terminal's internal engine.

High-Definition "Fish Tank" Resources

Since you prefer high-res local files over YouTube to save data, look for "4K Living Backgrounds" or "Cinemagraphs." Cinemagraphs are particularly good because they are designed to loop seamlessly, so you won't see a "jump" when the jellyfish video restarts.

Would you like me to find a few high-quality sources where you can download royalty-free 4K aquatic loops for your background?

Finding high-quality, local video files that loop seamlessly is the best way to maintain that aesthetic without the constant data drain of streaming. Since you are looking for that specific "aquatic tank" feel, here are several reliable sources where you can download high-definition (HD and 4K) jellyfish and marine life loops:

1. Pexels & Pixabay (Free & High Quality)

These are excellent for finding royalty-free, high-resolution videos. They both offer a "Download" button where you can select specific resolutions (like 1080p or 4K) to save to your Mac.

  • Pexels: Search for "Jellyfish" or "Underwater." Pexels is known for very clean, artistic cinematography that looks great behind terminal text.
  • Pixabay: Similar to Pexels, but often has a wider variety of "darker" aquatic videos which are better for terminal backgrounds as they keep your text readable.

2. Videezy (Specialized in Loops)

Videezy is a great resource because many of their contributors upload "B-Roll" specifically designed to be looped.

  • Look for videos tagged with "Loop" or "Seamless." This ensures that when the video restarts in iTerm2, you won't see a jarring cut or a flash of black.

3. Mazwai

Mazwai focuses on "cinematic" free stock footage. If you want a background that feels more like a professional film than a home aquarium, this is a great spot. Their selection is hand-picked, so the quality is consistently high.

4. Archive.org (Pre-looped Content)

The Internet Archive has a massive collection of "Living Backgrounds." If you search for "Aquarium Loop" or "Jellyfish HD," you can often find long-form files (10–20 minutes) that you can download once and run for hours without the loop even being noticeable.

Tips for the Best "Terminal" Look:

  • Go Dark: Try to find videos with deep blue or black backgrounds. High-contrast jellyfish (bright neon on dark water) look the best because they won't wash out your terminal text.
  • File Format: Stick to .mp4 or .mov. macOS and iTerm2 handle these natively with the least amount of CPU usage.
  • Resolution Check: While 4K is beautiful, if you notice your Mac's fans spinning up while you're coding, try downloading the 1080p (Full HD) version instead. At terminal window sizes, the difference is often negligible, but it's much easier on your hardware.

Once you download your favorite, you can just point your iTerm2 profile to that local file, and it will keep your "fish tank" vibe running offline and at full resolution.

Since you’re using Fish, you actually have two great ways to do this. You can do it the "Fish way" (using their built-in web customizer) or the "Modern way" (using Starship, which is a bit more robust).

Option 1: The "Fish Way" (Fast & Visual)

Fish has a built-in web-based configuration tool that lets you pick a prompt that already includes Git status.

  1. In your terminal, type: fish_config
  2. A browser window will open. Click on the "Prompt" tab.
  3. Look for prompts like "Informative" or "Classic + Git". These will show your current branch name and even colored symbols if you have uncommitted changes.
  4. Click "Set Prompt" and then close the browser.

Option 2: The Starship Way (Recommended)

If you want a prompt that looks "premium"—very clean, fast, and packed with useful info (like your Python version or Node version when you're in those project folders)—Starship is the gold standard.

1. Install it:

brew install starship

2. Add it to your config: Use your new fishconf command to open your config and add this line to the very bottom:

starship init fish | source

3. Reload: Run fishup.

Why Starship is great for your workflow:

  • Context Awareness: If you are in a directory for your Math Education classes with LaTeX files, it stays minimal. If you jump into a CS project, it suddenly shows your Git branch and the version of Python or Java you’re using.
  • Error Indicators: If a command fails, the prompt symbol usually turns red, giving you an instant visual cue.
  • Customization: It’s incredibly easy to tweak via a starship.toml file if you ever want to change the symbols or colors.

What’s next?

You now have a terminal that looks and acts like a pro developer's environment. Since you mentioned you like hearing from a variety of perspectives and communities, we could:

  1. Explore fzf: This adds a "search engine" to your command history (huge for productivity).
  2. Set up "Functions": These are like abbreviations but can handle complex tasks (like creating a new folder and jumping into it instantly).

Which of those sounds more interesting to dive into?
